title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting host under user pbeesly
summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly obtained handles to lsass.exe with full-access masks from PowerShell processes on two hosts. On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16; the same access was recorded in Windows Security 4656 with AccessMask 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell Remoting) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29, also seen in Security 4656 with AccessMask 0x1f3fff. The call traces run through PowerShell/System.Management.Automation native images, consistent with in-memory LSASS credential dumping. This occurred in the middle of a pbeesly PowerShell toolkit session (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil) on scranton.

title: pbeesly PowerShell credential-collection toolkit on scranton (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell credential/collection toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 between 03:04 and 03:08 on 2020-05-02. Script blocks include Get-PrivateKeys (exports certificate private keys to .pfx using a hardcoded password), Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, and Invoke-Exfil, which compresses the Downloads directory into OfficeSupplies.7z and copies it to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav. This is credential access and staging activity by the same user whose PowerShell process opened LSASS with full access.

title: No NTDS / domain-database dumping observed
summary: No ntds.dit file access, no vssadmin/diskshadow/ntdsutil execution, and no NTDS-related file creation were found in sysmon, security, powershell or other datasets. The activity is confined to LSASS memory access and host-level credential collection, not domain controller database theft.

title: No DCSync observed
summary: No drsuapi/DCSync command lines, no lsadump script blocks, and no directory-replication abuse were found in sysmon or powershell datasets. No evidence of DCSync in this window.

title: Azure Network Watcher packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is legitimate platform monitoring, not adversary sniffing
summary: The only packet-capture activity in the dataset is the Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local. NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (parent C:\Windows\System32\services.exe, user SYSTEM) starts a capture via netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes traceFile=...etl' and manages ETW trace sessions with logman.exe (GAEvents/RTEvents, output to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\*.etl). All parent processes are Azure guest-agent components (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, services.exe) and the binaries live under C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher... and C:\WindowsAzure\Packages. This is the standard Azure VM network-capture/diagnostics agent, not an adversary sniffing tool. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap, no Npcap/WinPcap driver load, no pcap files, and no promiscuous-mode commands were observed on any host.

title: No sniffing tooling, capture drivers or pcap artifacts found on any host
summary: Searches for network-sniffing tooling across the Windows datasets returned no adversary capture activity: no process creation of tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap, no image load of npcap/pcap/winpcap drivers, no pcap/sniff/promiscuous strings in PowerShell script blocks, and no pcap files written. The only .etl files created are OS/Azure diagnostic logs (ProvTool, waasmedic, SleepStudy, WDI, DiagnosticLogCSP) written by System/svchost/ProvTool. The zeek ICMP connection check also returned zero hits. The technique is therefore not observed as attacker behaviour in this window.

title: Attacker activity in window is PsExec lateral movement and python C2, not network sniffing
summary: The genuine malicious activity in this window is unrelated to T1040: on scranton.dmevals.local, PsExec64.exe (parent powershell.exe, user pbeesly) repeatedly runs against \\NASHUA with plaintext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. On nashua.dmevals.local that python.exe (parent C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, user pbeesly) then opens hundreds of TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. This is lateral movement/execution and C2, not credential sniffing, so it does not satisfy T1040; it is noted here only to distinguish it from the benign capture activity.

title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) using reflective/injected code
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z. The CallTrace shows only ntdll.dll/KERNELBASE.dll followed by UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), indicating the calling code is not backed by a known module (reflectively loaded/injected code) — the classic signature of credential API hooking / in-memory credential theft. A second open with 0x1f3fff occurred at 03:05:16.623Z. This is the same host/user (pbeesly) that ran an obfuscated PowerShell script using GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle and a base64 shellcode blob.

title: Obfuscated PowerShell with reflective code loading and base64 shellcode on scranton
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (EventID 4104, ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f) that defines functions using Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle and DefineDynamicAssembly/DefineDynamicModule to build an in-memory delegate, then decodes a base64 byte array ([System.Convert]::FromBase64String) — a reflective shellcode loader. A child process was spawned as powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e <base64> whose parent command line was powershell.exe -c "Get-ItemPropertyValue 'HKLM:\\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' | Invoke-Expression", i.e. hidden encoded execution. This tooling is consistent with in-memory credential capture on the host.

title: Benign LSASS handle requests by system processes (svchost, Defender, Azure agents)
summary: The bulk of LSASS process-access events are legitimate: svchost.exe (0x1000, 216+30+28+12 events across scranton/newyork/nashua/utica), Microsoft Azure IaaSAntimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (0x1400), and MsMpEng.exe — all with normal module-backed call traces (ntdll/KERNELBASE/perfts/CorperfmonExt). Security 4656 handle requests to lsass.exe/SAM by SCRANTON$ (SYSTEM) and by lsass.exe itself are routine OS activity. These are not credential capture.

title: No keylogger-specific API usage observed
summary: No process-creation command lines or PowerShell script blocks referencing keylogging APIs (GetAsyncKeyState, SetWindowsHookEx, keylog) were found; the corresponding checks returned zero hits. The LSASS/winlogon/explorer process-access events observed are dominated by svchost.exe with 0x1000 and by the malicious PowerShell LSASS open already reported under T1056.004, not by a keyboard-capture hook.

The only authentication-related hits are benign: a Remote Desktop session logon succeeded for DMEVALS\pbeesly (event 21) and a Customer Experience Improvement Program logon notification (event 7001) on scranton. title: No MFA/smart-card/OTP interception artifacts; credential theft toolkit observed instead
summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other produced no evidence of MFA interception. All 297 successful logons (4624) are ordinary types (3 network=218, 5 service=61, 2 interactive=15, 10 RDP=2, 0=1) using Negotiate/Kerberos; the 218 Kerberos logons are machine-account (computer$) network logons on newyork.dmevals.local. The 15 explicit-credential logons (4648) are pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe and built-in DWM/UMFD/winlogon accounts. LSASS access (Sysmon 10, 326 events) is dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) — normal. Registry 'Credential' hits are CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManager service setup by lsass.exe/services.exe — benign OS activity. No smart-card, OTP, token-interception, or credential-provider tampering was observed. However, the same window contains genuine credential-access activity on scranton.dmevals.local by user pbeesly (a PowerShell toolkit psversion.ps1/readme.ps1 exporting machine certificate private keys, capturing keystrokes/clipboard/screenshots, and PowerShell.exe opening LSASS with full access 0x1FFFFF) — this is credential theft (T1552.004/T1056.001/T1003), not MFA interception, so it is reported here as context rather than as a T1111 hit.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:18 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) issued 36 HTTP requests to 192.168.0.4:80 using the Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 user agent, including OPTIONS and PROPFIND methods against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The server answered 401 Unauthorized, which is the classic forced-authentication pattern: the WebDAV redirector causes the Windows host to automatically send NTLM/Kerberos credentials to an attacker-controlled listener. All 36 WebDAV-method requests came from a single source, 10.0.1.4, to a single destination, 192.168.0.4, and 61 of 62 HTTP requests in the window used the WebDAV MiniRedir agent. This is consistent with an adversary coercing authentication from a compromised workstation to capture credential material.

A file literally named for a password database, produced by a Sysinternals access-enumeration tool run interactively by a user, is consistent with an adversary collecting unsecured credentials. The same user session also ran sdelete64.exe to securely wipe files (C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Draft.Zip, C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite.zip) and used PsExec64.exe with a plaintext password, indicating deliberate anti-forensics and credential handling.

This is credential material stored/used in files and command lines rather than a secure store.

title: SYSVOL GPO file access is normal machine-account Group Policy processing
summary: SMB/SYSVOL access to GPO files (gpt.ini, GptTmpl.inf, SecEdit, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT) was observed in both zeek (2020-04-30, observers simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan and bobs.bigwheel.local reading \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol) and windows.security 5145 events on newyork.dmevals.local. All 5145 subjects are machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$) performing routine Group Policy refresh, and the zeek smb_files records are SMB::FILE_OPEN of standard policy paths. No Groups.xml with cpassword was read by a user account, and no attacker process accessed SYSVOL. This is expected domain behaviour, not GPP credential harvesting.

title: Registry Password/Credential value writes are OS service activity
summary: The 17 Sysmon event-13 registry writes matching Password/Credential keys on nashua/scranton are all performed by legitimate system processes: svchost.exe writing HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups, lsass.exe writing DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled, services.exe writing CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys, and winlogon.exe writing Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. None represent an adversary storing or harvesting credentials in the registry.

title: Interactive PowerShell and WinRM host open LSASS with full-access masks (credential dumping pattern)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, a PowerShell process (C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe, PID 0xba0) running as user pbeesly requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff, which includes 'Read from process memory' and 'Duplicate handle into or out of process' — the access pattern used to read credential material out of LSASS. The same user pbeesly, via wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM remote shell, PID 0x1e28) on nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z, requested a handle to lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff, again including read-process-memory. These are the only two non-system processes in the dataset that opened LSASS with these high-privilege masks (the 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff buckets otherwise consist of csrss.exe/svchost.exe opening ordinary processes). The activity is part of a broader pbeesly intrusion on scranton/nashua that also includes encoded/hidden PowerShell, sdelete64 anti-forensic wiping, and exfiltration tooling.

title: LSASS handle requests by user processes (Credential Manager/DPAPI harvest mechanism) — no vault object access observed
summary: The LSASS handle requests with 0x1fffff (scranton, powershell.exe, pbeesly) and 0x1f3fff (nashua, wsmprovhost.exe, pbeesly) are the mechanism by which Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI secrets held in LSASS memory would be harvested, so they are relevant to T1555.004. However, no direct access to Credential Manager vault objects, DPAPI Protect/Credential/Vault object names, or cmdkey/vaultcmd execution was observed: the only credential-related object-access events on lsass.exe were from C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe (Azure guest log collection, benign) and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe, and the only 'Credential' string in windows.other was the benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' event on scranton. The credential-store-specific artifact is therefore not directly observed; the LSASS access is attributed to T1555 broadly.

title: No browser credential-store access observed
summary: No evidence of web-browser credential theft was found. Searches for browser credential artifacts (Login Data, logins.json, cookies) in Sysmon file-create events, for browser processes (chrome.exe/firefox.exe) as LSASS access targets, and for browser-credential strings in PowerShell script blocks and Windows security object-access events returned no hits. The only cookie-related file event was an INetCookies file under a LocalService package profile on scranton, which is normal OS/app behaviour.

title: PowerShell Remoting host on NASHUA opened LSASS with full-access mask 0x1f3fff
summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29.430Z, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the PowerShell Remoting host, running as SYSTEM) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff — a full-access mask consistent with reading/patching the authentication process rather than the benign 0x1000 query mask seen for svchost. The call trace shows the access originating from PowerShell management assemblies (Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), i.e. a PowerShell session. This wsmprovhost process was created at 03:09:23.885Z by svchost.exe under user pbeesly, immediately after pbeesly used PsExec64.exe from scranton.dmevals.local to reach \\NASHUA with explicit credentials. This is attacker-driven access to the LSASS authentication process.

title: PsExec with plaintext credentials used to move to NASHUA and install PSEXESVC
summary: From scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly repeatedly launched C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\PsExec64.exe with the command line '"C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\PsExec64.exe" -accepteula \\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe' (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42). Each run caused the PSEXESVC service to be installed on nashua.dmevals.local (ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, demand start) and PSEXESVC.exe to execute as SYSTEM, which then produced 4648 explicit-credential logons for pbeesly. This is the credential-reuse/lateral-movement context in which the LSASS access occurred.

title: Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script with hardcoded credentials on SCRANTON
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:08:02Z, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block defining 'function Invoke-Exfil' (ScriptBlock ID b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1). title: Routine LSASS handle access by svchost and security agents (benign baseline)
summary: The bulk of the 326 LSASS-access events are benign: 289 from C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe and 28 from Microsoft Azure security/telemetry agents (AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe), overwhelmingly with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) or 0x1400. These are normal Windows service and AV/telemetry reads of LSASS, not authentication-process modification. The two powershell.exe LSASS accesses on scranton (0x1000, call trace through System.ni.dll) are likewise low-privilege query access.

title: Benign cryptdll/samlib/samcli image loads into normal Windows processes
summary: The 77 image-load hits for lsass/cryptdll/sam/msv1_0 are ordinary Microsoft-signed DLL loads (cryptdll.dll 'Cryptography Manager', samlib.dll 'SAM Library DLL', samcli.dll 'Security Accounts Manager Client DLL') into legitimate processes such as SearchProtocolHost.exe, SearchFilterHost.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, svchost.exe, dsregcmd.exe and powershell.exe. No unsigned or non-Microsoft module was loaded into LSASS, so this does not indicate authentication-process modification.

title: Benign LSA registry writes by lsass.exe and password-expiry notifications
summary: Registry writes touching LSA/password keys are normal OS behaviour: lsass.exe writing HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\ProductType, LsaCfgFlagsDefault and LsaPid on scranton, svchost.exe writing IdentityCRL ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups, and winlogon.exe writing the per-user PasswordExpiryNotification NotShownReason. No Notification Packages (password filter DLL) or NetworkProvider value was modified, so no T1556.002/T1556.008 persistence was established.

title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity; observed credential theft is PsExec-based lateral movement, not AiTM
summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioned in the middle of network traffic. The only credential-related activity is plaintext-credential lateral movement: on scranton.dmevals.local user pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA with explicit credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, which installed the PSEXESVC service on nashua.dmevals.local. That is T1021.002/T1078/T1003 territory, not T1557. Object-access stacking (4663/4670/4656) shows only routine processes (powershell, svchost, WmiPrvSE, services, lsass) touching Key/Token/File objects, and Sysmon network connections (event 3) show normal domain traffic (LDAP 389, Kerberos 88, SMB 445, DNS 53) with no unexpected relay host.

title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; DNS/WPAD lookups are routine and unanswered
summary: Name-resolution activity is normal. Zeek DNS shows wpad.dmevals.local queried by 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 returning NXDOMAIN (routine WPAD auto-discovery with no rogue WPAD responder answering), plus ordinary single-label NetBIOS-style lookups for SCRANTON/NASHUA and LDAP SRV records. Sysmon event 22 query names are all legitimate (host names, microsoft.com/azureedge telemetry, ocsp.digicert.com). No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tooling appears in PowerShell script blocks, and no SMB relay destination stands out: SMB (445) connections are between domain hosts (e.g. 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.5/10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4) with normal machine-account logons (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$).

title: No ARP cache poisoning; duplicate MACs are separate connections / lab placeholder
summary: Zeek conn records show host 10.0.1.4 reaching 10.0.1.6 with two different source MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and a responder MAC of 12:34:56:78:9a:bc. These are distinct connections at distinct timestamps, not one MAC claiming multiple IPs simultaneously, and 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic/placeholder address rather than a real gratuitous-ARP spoof. No ARP-poisoning tooling (arp/netsh interface) appears in PowerShell script blocks, and no network-configuration object tampering is visible in the 4663/4670/4656 object-access events.

title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP-related telemetry present
summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 absent from the code distribution), no PowerShell script block references DHCP, and the zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/smb_mapping/weird/notice/pe). Sysmon network connections show no DHCP ports 67/68. The technique is therefore not observable in this dataset rather than positively benign.

title: No Kerberos ticket theft or forging observed; LSASS accesses are legitimate system processes
summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon and zeek there is no evidence of Kerberos ticket theft or forging. The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local are normal KDC-issued tickets (AES256, TicketOptions 0x40810000/0x60810010 = forwardable/renewable TGT renewal), and the 4768 AS-REQs all carry PreAuthType=2 (pre-authentication required). LSASS handle accesses with elevated masks (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff, 0x101001) come from legitimate Windows components (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, svchost.exe) and from PowerShell/wsmprovhost whose surrounding activity is exfiltration, not ticket manipulation. No ticket-forging or roasting tooling was found.

title: No golden-ticket indicators: no RC4 downgrade and no anomalous krbtgt service tickets
summary: All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (event 4769) on newyork.dmevals.local use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), with no RC4 (0x17/0x18) downgrade that would suggest a forged golden ticket. The three krbtgt service-ticket requests (by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL) carry TicketOptions 0x60810010, consistent with legitimate TGT renewal rather than forged-ticket use. No golden-ticket forging tooling was found in PowerShell script blocks.

title: No silver-ticket indicators: all service tickets are KDC-issued with normal options
summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local target machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 and standard TicketOptions (0x40800000/0x40810000/0x60810010). There is no evidence of service tickets being used without corresponding KDC validation, and no silver-ticket tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS requests for SPNs and no roasting tooling
summary: No Kerberos service-ticket requests used RC4 encryption (all 4769 events are 0x12/AES256), which is the hallmark of Kerberoasting. The PowerShell script blocks contain no Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus content. The only notable PowerShell activity on scranton.dmevals.local by user pbeesly is an exfiltration script (Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads and copying to a WebDAV share), which is unrelated to Kerberoasting.

title: PowerShell script exported all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local

This is direct theft of authentication certificates and their private keys (T1649). The export is corroborated by Sysmon: powershell.exe read HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob and ...\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646\Blob at 03:04:57, and wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57.460. The activity is preceded (02:58:44) by a hidden, execution-policy-bypassed PowerShell launched by control.exe that decodes a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEXes it, indicating an initial stager on the same host/user. The certificate registry writes on other hosts (svchost.exe/lsass.exe/taskhostw.exe touching AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS stores) are normal OS certificate-store maintenance and are not attributed to the attacker.

Kerberos AS-REQ (event 4768) activity in windows.security is limited to the account pbeesly (9 requests) and the machine account SCRANTON$ (5 requests), all with Status 0x0 from internal addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 on newyork.dmevals.local — ordinary domain logon traffic, not certificate-based authentication abuse. The certificate/crypto registry writes in windows.sysmon are dominated by OS components (svchost.exe, lsass.exe, taskhostw.exe, smss.exe) touching AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS PhysicalStores and SymbolicLinkValue keys, i.e. routine certificate-store maintenance. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net, conn.sons.info) are external TLS server certificates from a non-overlapping window and show no forged authentication certificates. None of these constitute attacker certificate theft or forging.
